lines.text: Once the land of incense and the Queen of Sheba, later divided, united and torn by war. This is the story of Yemen.
Three thousand years ago, the kingdom of Saba grew rich on the incense trade, the Sheba of the old stories.
After it came the Himyarites, the last great kingdom of ancient Yemen, which ruled for more than six centuries.
With Islam, imams came to rule the north for a thousand years. In 1918 their realm became the Mutawakkilite Kingdom.
In the south, Britain had taken the port of Aden in 1839, and from 1937 ruled it as a colony of its own.
Ali Abdullah Saleh, born in 1947, would rise to rule Yemen for thirty-three years.
In 1962 the north's imam was overthrown, and a civil war between royalists and republicans lasted eight years.
Meanwhile the British left the south in 1967, and South Yemen became a socialist state, the only one in the Arab world.
Tawakkol Karman, born in 1979, would become a journalist and a voice of the Arab Spring, and win the Nobel Peace Prize.
In 1986 a new dam was raised at Marib, near the ruins of the great ancient dam that had once watered the kingdom of Saba.
In 1990 the two halves came together, and the Republic of Yemen was born at the south-west tip of Arabia.
North and South joined in May that year, ending a division that had lasted for generations.
Around 2000 the Houthi movement grew in the far north, a force that would one day seize the capital.
In 2011 the Arab Spring reached Yemen. Crowds filled the streets, and Saleh at last gave up power.
But in 2014 the Houthis took Sanaa, and the country fell into a civil war that drew in its neighbours.
The war brought famine and cholera, one of the worst humanitarian crises of this century.
From 2023 the Houthis attacked ships in the Red Sea, and much of the world's trade had to sail the long way around Africa.
From the incense kingdoms to a land at war, Yemen's story waits for peace.
